questions.stem_markdown: A parent in a Sydney adolescent clinic asks why the doctor is asking about sexuality during a routine health review when there is no known STI or pregnancy concern. What is the **best explanation** based on the notes?

options.text: Sexual health mainly means the absence of sexually transmitted infection
Sexual health is a state of physical, emotional, mental, and social wellbeing related to sexuality
Sexual health only becomes relevant once a young person is planning pregnancy
Sexual health questions are mainly for adult medicine rather than adolescent care
Sexual health is separate from general adolescent wellbeing

questions.explanation_markdown: The Louisa notes define **sexual health** as a state of **physical, emotional, mental, and social wellbeing related to sexuality**. This means it is broader than infection or pregnancy alone and is relevant to routine adolescent care.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes define sexual health more broadly than infection status alone.
why_others_wrong.C: The source material does not restrict sexual health to pregnancy planning.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes place adolescent sexual health within adolescent medicine, not only adult care.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes explicitly connect sexual health with broader wellbeing.

key_takeaways: Sexual health is broader than STI screening or pregnancy prevention alone.
The notes frame sexual health as part of overall adolescent wellbeing.
Routine adolescent care can appropriately include sexual health discussion.

questions.stem_markdown: A 15-year-old asks a clinician in NSW, "Does the law mean that any sexual activity before 16 is automatically a crime?" Which reply best matches the notes?

options.text: Yes. Any sexual activity involving a person under 16 is always a crime, regardless of age difference
No. The notes describe a defence if both people are 14 or over and the age difference is 2 years or less
No. Sexual activity is always lawful from age 15 in NSW
Yes, unless both families agree to the relationship
No. The only age threshold that matters is 18

questions.explanation_markdown: The Louisa notes state that in NSW, while the age of consent is 16, **consent to sexual activity with a person under 16 can be a defence to sexual crimes if both people are 14 or over and the age difference is 2 years or less**. This makes the answer more nuanced than a simple yes-or-no rule.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes include a close-in-age defence, so the rule is not this absolute.
why_others_wrong.C: The notes state that the age of consent is 16, not 15.
why_others_wrong.D: Family agreement is not the note-based legal criterion.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes specifically discuss age 16 and the close-in-age defence, so 18 is not the only threshold mentioned.

key_takeaways: The notes describe the NSW age-of-consent framework in a nuanced way.
A close-in-age defence is specifically mentioned for some under-16 situations.
Clinical communication should be accurate without oversimplifying the law.

questions.stem_markdown: A school nurse says condom and protection counselling should mainly focus on younger adolescents because older teenagers in relationships are less of a concern. Which correction best matches the notes?

The notes say condom use improves steadily with age, so counselling can be de-emphasised later in adolescence
The notes state relationship status removes the need for protection counselling
The notes indicate younger adolescents are the only group with important sexual health risk
The notes suggest sexual health counselling should focus on social media rather than protection

questions.explanation_markdown: The Louisa notes state that **older adolescents have more unprotected sexual intercourse than younger adolescents**, possibly linked to **relationship status**. This directly supports ongoing protection counselling in older teens rather than shifting attention away from them.

why_others_wrong.B: This is the opposite of the trend described in the notes.
why_others_wrong.C: The source material does not say relationship status removes the need for counselling about protection.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes do not limit sexual health risk to younger adolescents only.
why_others_wrong.E: Social media is mentioned in the notes, but it does not replace counselling about unprotected sex.

key_takeaways: Older adolescents can still be an important group for protection counselling.
Relationship status may be linked to more unprotected intercourse in the notes.
Clinicians should not assume age or relationship status removes sexual health risk.

why_others_wrong.E: The HIV-knowledge point comes from a different issue and does not explain the emotional-impact concern here.

key_takeaways: The notes do not support assuming sexual experiences are usually emotionally positive.
Wellbeing and pleasure are relevant parts of adolescent sexual health assessment.
Risky sexual behaviour includes impacts on mental health and wellbeing.

questions.stem_markdown: A parent says sexually oriented content on social media must be the single cause of their teenager's recent sexual behaviour. What is the **best explanation** from the notes?

The notes say the relationship is sketchy and probably bidirectional, so simple causal assumptions should be avoided

The notes say social media exposure fully explains risky sexual behaviour without any other psychosocial factors
The notes say social media behaviour matters only in adults

why_others_wrong.A: The notes do not describe a certain one-way causal relationship.
why_others_wrong.C: The notes actually say sexually oriented social media behaviour is common.
why_others_wrong.D: The source material specifically avoids that kind of simple explanation.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes discuss this in adolescents, not only adults.

key_takeaways: The notes do not support simplistic cause-and-effect assumptions about sexualized media exposure.

Clinical discussion should stay nuanced and context-aware.

questions.stem_markdown: Which background pattern should most alert a clinician to a **higher likelihood of risky sexual behaviour** based on the notes?

options.text: Strong parental monitoring, good school attendance, stable self-esteem, and no other risk behaviours
Poor parental monitoring, frequent time home alone, low self-esteem, poor mental health, and other risky behaviour
High HIV knowledge, good family relationships, and regular school attendance
A stable peer group, positive family relationships, and strong academic engagement
No early dating, good self-efficacy, and strong school connection

questions.explanation_markdown: The CAH Bible lists several predictors of risky sexual behaviour, including **poor parental monitoring**, **time home alone**, **poor quality family relationships**, **poor mental health**, **low self-efficacy and self-esteem**, poor school engagement, and **other risky behaviour**. Option B best matches that pattern.

why_others_wrong.A: These are more protective than concerning when compared with the note-based predictors.
why_others_wrong.C: High knowledge and good family and school supports do not match the main predictor pattern listed.
why_others_wrong.D: This option describes supports rather than recognised predictors of risky sexual behaviour.
why_others_wrong.E: The CAH Bible lists the opposite pattern as concerning, not protective factors like these.

key_takeaways: Risky sexual behaviour is shaped by psychosocial context as well as immediate choices.
The notes highlight family, school, self-esteem, mental health, and co-existing risk behaviours.
Screening should look beyond the sexual act itself.

questions.stem_markdown: A 16-year-old with ADHD describes impulsive sexual decisions that they later regret. Which note-based interpretation is **best**?

options.text: ADHD is unlikely to be relevant because risky sexual behaviour is mainly determined by relationship status alone
ADHD can exacerbate risky sexual behaviour because conditions that increase impulsivity may worsen this vulnerability
ADHD protects against risky sexual behaviour because it usually delays sexual activity
ADHD matters only if the adolescent is younger than 14 years old
ADHD is relevant only when there is already a confirmed STI

questions.explanation_markdown: The Louisa notes state that risky sexual behaviour is driven by developmental and psychosocial vulnerabilities and that it can be **exacerbated by conditions that increase impulsivity, e.g. ADHD**. That makes ADHD clinically relevant in this scenario.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes do not reduce risky sexual behaviour to relationship status alone.
why_others_wrong.C: The source material does not describe ADHD as protective here.
why_others_wrong.D: The ADHD point is not limited to those younger than 14 in the notes.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes discuss ADHD as a vulnerability factor, not only after an STI is already present.

key_takeaways: Impulsivity can amplify sexual risk in adolescence.
The notes specifically name ADHD as a possible exacerbating factor.
Assessment should consider neurobehavioural as well as social contributors.

why_others_wrong.E: The notes focus on sexual acts and age of consent, not mere discussion of feelings.

Focus narrowly on whether the adolescent feels good after sex and avoid talking about pregnancy or STI risk
Broaden counselling and follow-up because the pattern matches risky sexual behaviour linked to unplanned pregnancy and STI risk
Avoid further sexual health discussion unless the adolescent already has STI symptoms
Conclude that the main issue is social media rather than sexual health risk

why_others_wrong.A: The pattern described fits the note-based definition of risky sexual behaviour, so reassurance alone is too limited.
why_others_wrong.B: Wellbeing matters, but the notes also specifically identify pregnancy and STI risk in this pattern.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes do not say sexual health discussion should wait for symptoms.
why_others_wrong.E: Social media may be relevant in some contexts, but the main note-based issue here is the risky sexual behaviour described.

key_takeaways: Multiple partners over a short period and poor condom use are note-based markers of risky sexual behaviour.
Follow-up should address both STI and unplanned pregnancy risk.
Risk should not be dismissed as ordinary experimentation when the pattern clearly matches the notes.

questions.stem_markdown: A school-based clinician reviews a survey showing students can answer most HIV questions correctly but struggle when asked about common STIs. What is the **best educational follow-up** based on the notes?

Shift away from sexual health and teach only relationship skills
Prioritise more STI-focused education, because the notes say HIV knowledge is high but STI knowledge is poor
Stop school-based teaching and wait until students present with symptoms
Focus only on age-of-consent law because knowledge gaps about infection are minor

questions.explanation_markdown: The CAH Bible notes that **HIV knowledge is high, but STI knowledge is poor**. A school-based sexual health response should therefore include stronger STI-focused education rather than assuming infectious-disease knowledge is already adequate.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes specifically identify an ongoing STI knowledge gap, so reducing education would not fit the source material.
why_others_wrong.B: Relationship skills may still matter, but the note-based gap described here is STI knowledge.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes support recognising knowledge gaps earlier rather than waiting for symptomatic presentations.
why_others_wrong.E: The source material specifically highlights STI knowledge as the educational deficit here.

key_takeaways: Knowledge about HIV and knowledge about other STIs are not the same.
The notes identify poor STI knowledge as an important educational gap.
Follow-up education should match the gap that was actually found.

questions.stem_markdown: Which scenario is **least consistent** with the note-based definition of risky sexual behaviour?

options.text: A young person has sexual intercourse at an early age without protection
A young person has several partners over a short period and uses condoms inconsistently
A young person has sex that affects their mental health and gives no pleasure
A young person has sexual behaviour that increases the risk of STI or unplanned pregnancy
A young person has consensual sex with condom or contraceptive use and no reported wellbeing impact

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes describe risky sexual behaviour as behaviour that leads to **unplanned pregnancy or STI**, includes **early sexual intercourse debut**, **multiple partners over a short time**, **poor condom or contraceptive use**, and behaviour that harms **mental health and wellbeing**, including sex **without pleasure**. Option E is the least consistent with that pattern.

why_others_wrong.A: Early sexual intercourse debut is specifically listed in the CAH Bible as part of risky sexual behaviour.
why_others_wrong.B: Multiple partners over a short time and poor condom use are both note-based markers of risky sexual behaviour.
why_others_wrong.C: The Louisa notes specifically include behaviour affecting mental health and wellbeing, including sex without pleasure.
why_others_wrong.D: This directly matches the core note-based definition of risky sexual behaviour.

key_takeaways: Risky sexual behaviour is defined by both health risk and wellbeing impact in the notes.
Pregnancy and STI risk are important, but not the only concerns.
Protected consensual sexual activity without reported wellbeing harm is the least consistent with the risky pattern described.
